guideTitle: Best Rice Cookers for Brown Rice (2026)
metaTitle: Best Rice Cookers for Brown Rice (2026)
metaDescription: Six rice cookers that cook brown rice properly, from sensor and fuzzy logic digitals to mini cookers, with soak, water ratio and bran notes explained.
expertTake: The AROMA CoreCoat digital cooker is the best brown rice pick because its sensor control, ceramic pot and 15 hour delay timer are built around whole grains. The AROMA 8-cup multicooker is the value pick when you want a brown rice preset and a steam tray without a premium. Skip a plain one-switch cooker for brown rice, because it ends the cycle too early for the bran layer.
introParagraphs: Brown rice keeps its bran, a waxy layer that blocks water and slows cooking. The grain needs more water, a longer time and ideally a soak, which is why a cooker built for white rice often leaves brown rice hard in the center or gummy on the outside.

A good brown rice cooker either offers a dedicated program, adapts its heat with sensors or fuzzy logic, or gives you a timer to soak before the cook. We evaluated six on those points, plus pot size and how well each handles a typical batch of two to four cups.

products.name: AROMA CoreCoat Digital 8-Cup Cooker for Brown Rice, Ceramic Pot
products.description:
The maker markets this cooker for brown rice, and the design backs it up. A digital panel offers a brown rice program next to white rice, quinoa, bulgur and a fast flash mode, with sensor control adjusting the cook. The 15 hour delay timer is the useful detail, since it lets brown rice soak in the pot before the heat starts.

The pot holds 4 raw cups, which makes 8 cooked, so it suits two to four people. The CoreCoat ceramic surface avoids fluoropolymers and cleans well after the sticky bran water that brown rice leaves behind. It is a small step up in cost tier from the plain digital model in the same family, and the timer is the main reason to take it.

Soak the pot after each cook, because bran starch dries into a film. Use a plastic paddle, wipe the panel with a damp cloth and rinse the vent. If you use the long delay, start with room-temperature water and keep the cooker away from a hot window, since a long warm soak can turn brown rice sour. Quinoa and bulgur on the same panel make the cooker useful on the days you want something other than rice, and the flash mode is better kept for white rice, since brown rice needs the long cook to soften. Replacement CoreCoat pots are the part to check for before you buy, because the coating is the first wear item.
products.bestFor: Households that eat brown rice weekly and want a soak timer.
pros: Dedicated brown rice program with sensor control
Delay timer up to 15 hours for soaking
cons: Four raw cups is small for big families

products.name: AROMA 8-Cup Digital Rice and Grain Multicooker, 2 Qt
products.description:
This is the straightforward way to get a brown rice preset. One-touch digital controls offer white rice, brown rice, steam and oatmeal, and the unit switches to Keep Warm automatically after the cycle. A BPA-free steam tray rides above the pot for vegetables, meat or dumplings.

It does not have the sensor control or the delay timer of the CoreCoat digital, so the soak has to be done by hand: wash the rice, cover it with water for thirty minutes and then press the brown rice button. For people who do not mind that extra step, it delivers the preset at a lower cost tier. The 2 quart pot is the same size as the premium model.

Because there is no timer, brown rice here is a planned meal rather than a set-and-forget one. Wash the tray after steaming and rinse the vent. The nonstick pot should be treated gently, and a bran film on the pot wall is a sign to soak, not scrub. Oatmeal is the other preset worth using, and it makes the same cooker a breakfast machine on mornings when you want a hot cereal. Check that the tray sits level on the pot rim before cooking, because a tilted tray lets steam leak past and shortens the cook.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a brown rice button at a modest cost tier.
pros: 2 quart pot for two to four people

products.name: Martha Stewart 8-Cup Cooked Rice Cooker, Fuzzy Logic, Ceramic Pot

specList.label: Modes
specList.value: White, sushi, brown, quinoa, grains, steam, steel-cut oats

products.description:
This cooker is the one with real adaptive heat at a family size. Nine cooking modes include white rice, sushi rice, brown rice, quinoa, grains, steam, steel-cut oats and quick cook, and smart fuzzy logic adjusts temperature and time. The removable pot is a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick.

Fuzzy logic is the right match for brown rice, because the bran layer makes cooking times vary by grain type and age. It can compensate where a fixed program cannot, which is why a batch of old, dry brown rice does not come out hard. The brand name is better known for housewares than for rice cookers, so the long-term service record is thin, and the warranty deserves attention.

Let the brown rice rest with the lid closed for ten minutes after the program ends, then fluff. Wipe the lid vent and the pot rim each time. The steel-cut oat mode is a good second use, since it needs the same gentle, long heat. The sushi mode is a bonus for the occasional white short grain dinner, though the cooker is happiest with whole grains. Keep the measuring cup in the drawer next to the cooker so the water lines always match the cup you use.
products.bestFor: Families that want adaptive heat and many grain modes.
pros: Smart fuzzy logic adjusts time and temperature
Nine modes including brown rice and quinoa
cons: Brand has a short rice cooker record

products.name: Toshiba 3-Cup Uncooked Small Rice Cooker, 8 Functions, LCD

specList.label: Sensing
specList.value: Moisture sensing adjusts heat and time

products.description:
Toshiba's small cooker offers eight programmable functions, including white rice, quick cook and brown rice, on an LCD panel. It senses moisture in the rice and adjusts temperature and cooking time, which gives it an edge over simple preset cookers for whole grains. The 3 cup uncooked pot suits one to three people.

It is the compact choice for a person who wants brown rice in small amounts, and a small pot has an advantage here: the bran layer cooks evenly when the batch is shallow. The limit is capacity, since a family of four will need two batches.

The panel should be wiped, not rinsed. Let the pot cool before washing, and clean the lid and vent at the same time. For the best texture, soak the brown rice for thirty minutes and use the brown program, then let it sit covered for several minutes. Because the panel has a quick cook function, it is tempting to use it on brown rice, but that mode is meant for white rice and will leave the center of brown grains hard. A level measure of rice and the line for brown rice, not white, is the single most useful habit with this cooker.
products.bestFor: One to three people who cook brown rice in small batches.
pros: Moisture sensing adjusts heat and time
LCD panel is easy to read
cons: Too small for a family of four

products.name: Narcissus 3.5-Cup Uncooked Rice Cooker, 1.8 L, White and Brown
products.description:
Narcissus sells this mini cooker for white and brown rice, oatmeal and quinoa, with a delay start and automatic warm. The 3.5 cup uncooked capacity gives seven cups cooked from a 1.8 liter pot. It is made for one to three people.

The delay start is the feature that matters for brown rice, because the long soak improves tenderness, though it is only as good as your control over the room temperature. A newer brand, it lacks the long record of the established lines, so treat it as a budget pick with a warranty to read.

Wash the pot by hand and check the lid vent after each cook. Use the delay start for a soak of an hour or two, not overnight, since brown rice in warm water for a long time may ferment. A dry pot base protects the sensor. If the first batch of brown rice comes out too firm, add a tablespoon or two of water for the next one instead of changing programs. Small cookers like this heat quickly, so give the rice a few extra minutes of rest after the cycle for the center to finish steaming.
products.bestFor: Small households that want a brown rice program at a low tier.
pros: Brown rice program with delay start
cons: Newer brand with a short record
Overnight delay can ferment brown rice

products.name: Cosori 10-Cup Fuzzy Logic Cooker, Ceramic Pot, Texture Options

specList.label: Brown rice
specList.value: Several white and brown texture options

products.description:
Cosori is the large pot for brown rice. Fuzzy logic with several white and brown rice texture options lets you choose how firm the grain ends up, and a delay start gives time for a soak. The ceramic pot handles the sticky bran film better than a worn nonstick one.

The controller is the point, and the pot size is the cost. A 10 cup pot is too big for one cup of brown rice and best used for four cups and up. Against the Martha Stewart cooker, it offers more capacity and more texture choices, while the Martha Stewart is closer to an 8 cup family size.

Let the cycle finish and the keep warm run for ten minutes before opening. Soak the pot after serving, and use only plastic tools in the ceramic. If the display shows an error, check that the pot sits flat and the base is dry. Cooking only two cups of brown rice in this large pot is possible with the fuzzy logic, but the thin layer can dry at the edges, so add a little extra water. Portion leftovers into containers and freeze them flat, since brown rice reheats well in a microwave with a splash of water.
products.bestFor: Large families that want texture control for brown rice.
pros: Fuzzy logic with brown rice texture options
cons: Large pot is wasteful for small batches

buyingCriteria.explanation: The bran layer blocks water, so brown rice needs more water, a longer cook and ideally a soak of about 30 minutes to an hour. A cooker that ends at the first sign of dry plate, like a basic thermal switch, often stops too early. Choose a cooker with a brown program, sensors or fuzzy logic. A white rice cycle on brown rice is the number one cause of the crunchy centers people complain about, and it is a settings problem, not a rice problem.

The AROMA 8-cup multicooker has a brown preset, the Toshiba senses moisture and the Martha Stewart and Cosori use fuzzy logic. Presets save guesswork, and sensors adapt to the actual grain. Sensors and fuzzy logic are better for batches that vary in size.

The AROMA CoreCoat digital offers a delay up to 15 hours and the Narcissus and Cosori have delay starts. A soak of one to two hours improves tenderness. Overnight soaking in a warm kitchen is risky, since brown rice can ferment.

Brown rice usually takes between two and two and a quarter parts water per part rice, depending on the variety. The water lines in cookers are tuned for white rice, so check the manual for the brown line. If the rice is firm, add a splash of water and run the cycle again.

A 4 raw cup pot like the AROMA digital models and Martha Stewart cooks two to four cups well. A 10 cup Cosori suits larger batches. Small batches in a big pot dry out at the edges. Because brown rice is bulkier per serving than white, plan on a cup of raw rice for every two to three people, and size the pot with that in mind.
Brown rice leaves a bran starch film that clings to the pot wall. A ceramic or nonstick pot releases it when soaked. Use plastic tools and a soft sponge.

cards.label: Preset
cards.text: The AROMA 8-cup multicooker and Narcissus run a fixed brown rice program. They work well at normal loads and cost less.

cards.label: Adaptive
cards.text: The Toshiba sensing model and the fuzzy logic Martha Stewart and Cosori adjust to the grain and batch size. They are better when quantities vary.

howToChoose.note: Pick preset for a steady routine. Pick adaptive if batch sizes and grains vary.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A pot large enough to cook several servings and a warm mode that keeps rice from drying. Brown rice holds better than white in the refrigerator.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Cosori 10-Cup and the Martha Stewart 8-Cup are the best for batches, with the Cosori offering the biggest pot.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You eat brown rice several times a week and want consistent texture. The CoreCoat digital and fuzzy logic models repay that.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You eat brown rice occasionally. The AROMA 8-cup multicooker or Narcissus covers it.

maintenance.why: Bran starch dries into a film. Soaking loosens it without scraping.
Brown rice foams and can leave residue. A clean vent prevents sputtering.
Moisture upsets sensors and hisses on the plate.
Brown rice cooks longer and wears coatings. Replace flaking pots.

faq.q: Why is my brown rice hard?
faq.a: Usually too little water or too short a cook for the bran layer. Soak the rice, use the brown line and run a program built for it.

faq.q: Do I need to soak brown rice?
faq.a: It is not required, but a soak of 30 minutes to an hour improves tenderness. A delay timer makes it easy.

faq.q: How much water for brown rice?
faq.a: About two to two and a quarter parts water per part rice, though varieties differ. Check your cooker manual.

faq.q: Can I use a plain cooker?
faq.a: Yes with extra water and patience, but results are less consistent. A brown program or sensors help.

faq.q: How long does brown rice take?
faq.a: Programs run from about 40 minutes to over an hour, depending on soak and cooker. Plan ahead.

faq.q: Is brown rice worth the extra effort?
faq.a: Many people prefer its nutty flavor and chew. A cooker with a brown program makes it as easy as white rice.
